I implemented `plan_jobs` in `jobqueue.py` as a deterministic, dependency-aware topological scheduler using only the standard library (`collections.abc`, `dataclasses`, `heapq`, `typing`). The design runs three passes: pass 1 validates each entry (must be a `Job`, non-empty/unique non-blank string `id`, numeric `priority`, non-string iterable `depends_on`, collapsing duplicate entries so a repeated dependency can't inflate indegree and fake a cycle); pass 2 resolves references so forward-declared dependencies are legal; pass 3 runs Kahn's algorithm with a heap keyed on `(-priority, input_position)`, giving highest-priority-first with input order as a stable tie-break, and evaluating priority dynamically over the *currently ready* set so a blocked high-priority job never reserves its slot or preempts an already-ready one. When the heap empties early, an iterative white/grey/black DFS over only the still-blocked jobs reconstructs one concrete cycle (`a -> b -> c -> a`) and lists all blocked jobs separately, distinguishing genuine cycle members from jobs merely downstream of them. Both the scheduling loop and the cycle DFS are iterative so deep chains and cycles can't exhaust the stack, and no supplied `Job`, dependency list, or payload is ever mutated — including on error paths. I expanded the suite from 3 to 44 tests (via a shared `assert_valid_order` oracle) covering empty/generator/single-job input, id and dependency validation, forward deps, diamonds, fan-in, negative priorities, determinism, 2000-deep chains and cycles, and immutability. Three tests failed on the first run; all three were wrong expectations of mine, not implementation bugs (I had omitted `right` from a diamond whose consumer needs both branches, expected a blocked job to jump the ready queue, and contradicted the dependency rule in a tie case) — I re-derived each from the contract and corrected the expectations. Verification: `python3 -m unittest -v` from the task directory on Python 3.14.3 reports `Ran 44 tests ... OK`; I additionally cross-validated against an independent oracle on 3000 random DAGs (valid, dependency-respecting permutations) and 1000 random DAGs (deterministic and matching a brute-force greedy simulation), and documented all of this in `RESPONSE.md`.

**All deliverables completed:** `jobqueue.py` (implementation), `test_jobqueue.py` (44 passing tests), and `RESPONSE.md` (design, edge cases, exact verification command/result). All work stayed inside the task directory, and no network or third-party packages were used.
